titre: The bird we thought could never die out
accroche: In 1813, a flock of passenger pigeons takes more than three days to pass over Kentucky. A century later, the species is gone.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1813, in Kentucky, John James Audubon observes a flock of passenger pigeons so dense that it blots out the sky for more than three days of continuous passage. The species, Ectopistes migratorius, then numbers between three and five billion individuals: the most abundant bird in North America. Audubon himself judges that such abundance puts the species beyond any danger of extinction.

A century later, on September 1, 1914, Martha, the last known member of the species, dies at the Cincinnati Zoo. In between, commercial hunting, nets that captured up to 3,500 birds at once, and the disappearance of the beech and chestnut forests the species fed on made the population plummet. Around 1900, no wild nest is reported anymore.

## What hunting alone doesn't explain

Hunting explains the decline. It does not explain why the species, once down to a few thousand individuals, a number more than sufficient to sustain many other species, never recovered. Captive breeding attempts, notably at the Cincinnati Zoo, also fail: the birds refuse to reproduce in small groups.

The passenger pigeon lived and bred in immense colonies, sometimes several hundred nests in a single tree. A large colony protects each individual by sheer dilution: a predator can eat only a limited fraction of a flock of several million birds, and the bulk of the group gets through. It also makes foraging easier, since an immense flock spots a tree laden with beechnuts faster, and seems to have been necessary to trigger breeding itself. Below a certain density threshold, these advantages reverse: a small group exposes each bird more, finds food less well, and no longer breeds.

The zoologist W.C. Allee documented this mechanism as early as 1931; it now bears his name, the Allee effect. For many species, an individual's fitness, its chances of surviving and reproducing, does not increase continuously as the population shrinks and competition eases. Below a threshold, it decreases instead with density. A population then no longer needs to be rare to be doomed: it can still be there, by the thousands, and have already tipped over.

## A received idea that costs dearly in conservation

Audubon's intuition, that abundance protects, remains widespread. It partly explains why so many conservation programs step in only when a species becomes rare in the everyday sense of the term. The Allee effect says the opposite: the critical threshold can sit well above zero, and a population still made up of thousands of individuals may already have tipped into a decline that no protection against hunting is enough to reverse.

carte.punch: Three to five billion individuals were not enough to save the passenger pigeon from extinction.
carte.idee: In 1813, the most abundant bird in North America numbered in the billions. A century later, it was gone: below a certain density threshold, its colonies could no longer protect themselves from predators or reproduce. Abundance does not shelter a species.

quiz.question: Why was the passenger pigeon never able to recover once its population fell to a few thousand individuals?
choix: Because the species depended on very large colonies to protect itself and reproduce, an advantage that reverses below a threshold
Because commercial hunting continued without ever slowing, until the very last wild individual was captured
Because an epidemic spread through the last surviving groups, finishing off an already very fragile population
Because the beech and chestnut forests it fed on had completely disappeared from the continent
quiz.explication: Hunting and deforestation explain the decline, not the absence of recovery. The passenger pigeon needed immense colonies to dilute the risk of predation and to trigger its breeding; below a certain density threshold, these same mechanisms turn against it. This is the Allee effect, not a disease or a total disappearance of the forests.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did John James Audubon think about the species' future, after observing the 1813 flock?
choix: That it would disappear within the next fifty years if hunting continued
That such abundance put the species beyond any danger of extinction
That it would migrate to Europe to escape commercial hunting
That it had already begun to decline at the time of his observation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that Audubon himself judges that such abundance puts the species beyond any danger of extinction, a forecast that would prove false.

choix: Just one bird at a time, hunting remaining small-scale
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that commercial hunting used nets capable of capturing up to 3,500 birds at once, a factor in the species' rapid decline.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did captive breeding attempts, notably at the Cincinnati Zoo, fail?

Because the zoo's staff lacked training in ornithology
Because the last captive individuals were already too old to reproduce
Because the birds refuse to reproduce in small groups
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that captive breeding attempts fail because the birds refuse to reproduce in small groups.
